Name: Yat Lok Roast Goose
Location: G/F, Conwell House, 34-38 Stanley Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Family roast-goose shop founded in 1957, now a Michelin-starred counter. Quarter goose over lai fun in broth is the order; char siu and soy chicken also recommended. Why: Locally beloved siu mei institution; open daily, so workable on both holiday days. Cash only.

Name: Kam's Roast Goose
Location: G/F, Po Wah Commercial Centre, 226 Hennessy Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Third-generation roast goose house with about 30 seats; goose blood pudding and noodles tossed in goose fat are side highlights. Why: Michelin-starred siu mei with a 70-year family lineage; locally beloved, queues are normal.

Name: Kau Kee Restaurant
Location: 21 Gough Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: No-frills beef brisket and tendon noodle house trading since the 1930s, with shared tables and curry or broth options. Milk tea also recommended. Why: Old-school Central institution; cash only and queues of up to an hour or more.

Name: Lau Sum Kee Noodle (Fuk Wing Street)
Location: 82 Fuk Wing Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Since 1956; third generation still kneads dough with a bamboo pole. Shrimp-roe tossed noodles and prawn wonton noodles are the draws. Why: Locally beloved Sham Shui Po noodle house with Michelin recognition; a pillar of the bamboo-pole noodle craft.

Name: Dragons' Den
Location: Shop S02, 2F, Tin Ma Court Commercial Centre, 55 Chuk Yuen Road, Wong Tai Sin, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Retro mid-century dining room in a mall near Lion Rock reviving hard-to-find Cantonese dishes: baked egg omelette with fish tripe, dry-aged pear-wood-smoked squab, dim sum lunch. Why: One of six new Hong Kong Bib Gourmand entries in the 2026 guide (March 2026); a retro-themed room inside a housing-estate mall.

Name: Ho Ho Chak
Location: 9F, Nathan Hill, 38 Hillwood Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Chiu Chow restaurant run by three brothers who also wholesale seafood and fruit. Steamed pork patty with mud crab and fried omelette with dried radish. Why: New 2026 Bib Gourmand entry; modern-feeling Chiu Chow in TST.

Name: Lai's Kitchen
Location: 1F, Harvard Commercial Building, 105-111 Thomson Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Dai pai dong-inspired Cantonese room: budget rice and noodle dishes at lunch; wok stir-fries and claypot rice cooked to order at dinner, including three-treasure claypot. Why: New 2026 Bib Gourmand; part of the Flower Drum group. A tidy way to try winter claypot rice.

Name: Sing Heung Yuen
Location: 2 Mee Lun Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Roadside dai pai dong on Mee Lun Street, open since 1959, known for tomato soup noodles, egg and beef toasted sandwiches and crispy butter-honey bun. Why: Iconic surviving dai pai dong in Central; appears on Time Out's July 2026 dai pai dong list.

Name: ChorLand Cookfood Stall
Location: G/F, Po Kwong Building, 2C Ma Hang Chung Road, To Kwa Wan, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Dai pai dong-style stall in To Kwa Wan, listed first on Time Out's July 2026 dai pai dong list: sweet and sour pork, clams in black bean sauce, salt and pepper corn, pork-lard soy rice. Why: Newer wave of dai pai dong in the 13 Streets area; wok-hei cooking.

Name: Haiphong Road Temporary Cooked Food Hawker Bazaar
Location: Haiphong Road Temporary Market, Haiphong Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cluster of cooked-food stalls: satay beef noodles, pork chops, Hainan chicken rice, beef balls. Why: Cheap, local TST option away from the promenade crowds.

Name: Lok Hau Fook
Location: G/F, 1-3 Hau Wong Road, Kowloon City, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Chiu Chow restaurant founded 1954 with a dated interior: melon pancake, chicken dumplings, sugar-coated taro. Featured in the film Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In. Why: Heritage Chiu Chow in the old Walled City neighbourhood; a PolyU Aug 2026 heritage walk stops here, indicating it operates.

Name: Kwan Kee Claypot Rice
Location: 263 Queen's Road West, Sai Ying Pun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Charcoal-fired claypot rice with a crisp scorched base; long waits. Why: Locally loved winter institution; fits the season.

Name: Sheung Hei Claypot Rice
Location: 25 North Street, Kennedy Town, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Claypot rice specialist formerly Bib Gourmand; lap mei sausage and spare ribs, eel with field chicken. Weekend queues are long. Why: One of the most-cited winter claypot stops in the west.

Name: Ser Wong Fun
Location: 30 Cochrane Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Snake soup house founded in Guangzhou in 1895; also chicken and pig-liver-sausage claypot rice. Why: The classic winter snake soup stop; a 2026 hotel partnership suggests the brand is active.

Name: Luk Yu Tea House
Location: 24-26 Stanley Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Art Deco-era Cantonese teahouse (opened 1933) with wooden booths, ceiling fans and stained glass, serving traditional yum cha and a la carte Cantonese. Michelin's blurb singles out deep-fried chicken and fried beef noodles. Why: The last grand old-style Cantonese teahouse in Central; iconic for atmosphere, waiter-led service and old-school dim sum rather than for value. Locally beloved by regulars; expect a formal, sometimes brusque welcome for walk-ins.

Name: Tim Ho Wan (Sham Shui Po)
Location: 9-11 Fuk Wing Street, Sham Shui Po, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: The Michelin-recognised budget dim sum shop of the chain founded by ex-Four Seasons chefs: baked BBQ pork buns, shrimp dumplings, steamed beef balls with tangerine peel. Opened 2010 in Sham Shui Po. Why: The Michelin-cheap-dim-sum phenomenon started in this neighbourhood; it has held a Bib Gourmand for 17 straight years (2026 edition) and sits next to Fuk Wing Street's toy and wonton-noodle strip. Popular with visitors, so a 'famous but still good value' pick rather than a hidden one.

Name: Mak Man Kee Noodle Shop
Location: 51 Parkes Street, Jordan, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Family wonton-noodle shop (roots in a 1945 food cart): fat shrimp wontons in thin skin, springy duck-egg noodles, rich dried-flounder broth; noodles can be tossed in shrimp roe or oyster sauce. Why: Locally beloved Bib Gourmand and the benchmark for Cantonese wonton noodles; Michelin lists it open until 00:30, so it doubles as a late bowl. Cash only.

Name: Tsim Chai Kee Noodle (Wellington Street)
Location: 98 Wellington Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Small Wellington Street noodle shop for big fish-ball, beef-ball and shrimp wontons in clear broth with thin egg noodles; a choice of three toppings per bowl. Bib Gourmand in the 2026 Michelin list. Why: Quick, cheap, Michelin-recognised wonton-noodle stop in the middle of Central; popular with office workers and tourists, so locals' favourites may be elsewhere. Cash only.

Name: Hop Yik Tai
Location: 121 Kweilin Street, Sham Shui Po, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Sham Shui Po street-snack shop famed for freshly steamed, lard-scented rice rolls (cheung fun) with sesame, sweet and chilli sauces, plus fish balls, pork skin and braised radish. Why: Locally beloved, always-busy cheung fun counter; the classic cheap Sham Shui Po snack. Cash only.

Name: Trusty Congee King (Wan Chai)
Location: 7 Heard Street, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Long-running congee shop cooking its congee in fish broth: pork liver and scallop congee, poached grass-carp skin and sticky-rice dumplings with salted egg yolk are the recommended orders. Why: Locally reliable congee institution (Bib Gourmand in the 2026 list), open all day and handy as a warm breakfast or late snack on a cold December day.

Name: Australia Dairy Company
Location: 47 Parkes Street, Jordan, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Fast-turnover cha chaan teng famed for glossy scrambled eggs on toast, steamed egg custard and milk pudding, plus macaroni soup and milk tea. Waiters are famously brisk and tables are shared. Why: The canonical 'queue-for-scrambled-eggs' cha chaan teng; Michelin cites it among the traditional spots keeping the classic offerings alive. Popular with tourists, loved by locals for the speed and ritual.

Name: Kam Wah Cafe & Bakery
Location: G/F, 47 Bute Street, Prince Edward (Mong Kok), Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: 1970s cha chaan teng known for its fresh-baked pineapple bun with a slab of butter (bo lo yau), plus egg tarts, French toast and milk tea. Why: The stop for a proper pineapple bun with butter; locally beloved and heavily visited. A Sept 2026 Taiwanese-press roundup lists it as open 06:30-23:30, so it covers late-night supper too.

Name: Mido Cafe
Location: 63 Temple Street, Yau Ma Tei, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: A 1950 bing sutt with mosaic floor tiles, wooden booths and arched windows over Temple Street; baked pork chop rice, claypot dishes, milk tea and toasts. Why: One of the few surviving old-style bing sutt interiors, a retro-HK film-set staple. Food is average; the room is the reason.

Name: Tai Cheong Bakery (Lyndhurst Terrace)
Location: G/F, 35 Lyndhurst Terrace, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Hong Kong's most famous egg-tart bakery (from 1954): shortcrust egg tarts with a smooth, wobbly custard, plus butter-crust and milk-white variants and cookies. Why: The tart reportedly praised by the last governor; the Central flagship near the Mid-Levels Escalator is still listed in 2026 coverage. All Kowloon branches closed by Nov 2024 (about six remain city-wide).

Name: Kai Kai Dessert (Pitt Street, Jordan)
Location: G/F, 113-115 Pitt Street, Jordan, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Traditional sweet-soup shop (since the 1970s) known for stone-ground black sesame paste, almond cream and walnut cream, plus mango-pomelo-sago style desserts. The original Ning Po Street shop closed 17 Sep 2025 and relocated to Pitt Street. Why: Michelin-recognised for nine straight years as a street-food icon (Bib Gourmand in the 2026 list); a locally loved cult sweet-soup stop and open past midnight.

Name: Heartwarming (Prince Edward)
Location: 23 Yu Chau Street, Prince Edward, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Black-sesame specialist with two stone mills grinding at the door: hot sweet black sesame soup, ice cream, pudding and chewy sesame rolls. Why: A 2025 Bib Gourmand newcomer still listed in 2026; a modern take on the winter sweet soup, near Mong Kok.

Name: Fong Wing Kee Satay Beef Specialist
Location: G/F, 85-87 Hau Wong Road, Kowloon City, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Kowloon City institution (50+ years per Tatler) serving satay-broth hot pot with hand-cut beef and broad noodles, in the neighbourhood's Chiu Chow/Thai-influenced satay tradition. Why: Old-school, locally anchored hot pot for a cold December night, listed in Tatler Asia's Dec 2025 hot pot guide; pairs with a Kowloon City Thai crawl.

Name: Chuen Kee Seafood (Hoi Pong Street)
Location: 53 Hoi Pong Street, Sai Kung, New Territories, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Family-run waterfront seafood restaurant (since the 1980s) with a rooftop terrace by the Sai Kung quay: pick live fish from tanks, cooked as you choose; abalone and salt-and-pepper mantis shrimp are the highlights. Why: Classic Sai Kung seafood day-out, listed in the 2026 Michelin Guide. Sai Kung is also an easy base for Lei Yue Mun alternatives; busy on holiday weekends.

Name: Hyde Park Garden Seafood Restaurant
Location: 44 Hoi Pong Road Central, Lei Yue Mun, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Two-storey Lei Yue Mun seafood house that grew from a dai pai dong. Choose seafood from the owner's stall across the way and have it cooked for a fee; Michelin cites razor clams in black bean, fish-and-tofu soup and ginger-scallion abalone claypot. Why: The Lei Yue Mun pick-and-cook village ritual with a Michelin-listed kitchen; open to 23:00 so it works for a late dinner after Kowloon sightseeing.

Name: Lung King Heen
Location: 4/F, Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong, 8 Finance Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Harbour-view Cantonese restaurant in the Four Seasons, famous for refined dim sum lunch and double-boiled soups; Michelin's page shows two stars. Why: The splurge Cantonese meal: a dim sum lunch here is the established way to do high-end HK dining. Weekend lunch starts 11:30.

Name: BTS Food Station
Location: 11 Shing Nam Road, Kowloon City, Kowloon, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cheap Kowloon City Thai favourite: Hainan chicken rice, crispy pork knuckle, boat noodles, sizzling Thai oyster omelette and tom yum seafood pot. Why: Kowloon City is HK's 'Little Bangkok' via Thai Teochew immigrants; HK01 (31 Jul 2026) names BTS as one of the few Thai shops open to midnight, so it fits a late dinner.

Name: Lee Keung Kee Egg Waffles (North Point)
Location: 492 King's Road, North Point, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Original-flavour egg waffle (gai daan jai) shop, crisp outside and soft inside; has since opened extra branches in Tsim Sha Tsui and Po Lam. Why: A long-standing, locally cited egg waffle benchmark; use it alongside the Quarry Bay / North Point tram walk.

Name: Luk On Kui
Location: 2-3/F, 40-50 Des Voeux Road West, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Old-school trolley dim sum teahouse on two floors in Sheung Wan, formerly Lin Heung Kui and renamed Luk On Kui when it reopened in 2024. Carts of siu mai, beef balls, sa yung and egg tarts roll through a loud, shared-table room. Why: One of the last places in the city still serving dim sum from pushcarts in a raucous traditional hall; a 'point at the cart' experience rather than a menu one.

Name: Lin Heung Tea House (Tsim Sha Tsui)
Location: 1-2/F, Cheung Lee Commercial Building, 25 Kimberley Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Kowloon branch of the century-old Lin Heung teahouse, opened in May 2025 across two floors and open 24 hours. Dim sum comes round on trolleys alongside traditional teaware, with a stamp card for the first steamer. Why: The only round-the-clock trolley dim sum in the city, and the way to get the Lin Heung experience on the Kowloon side at any hour, including Christmas night.

Name: Choi Lung Restaurant
Location: 2 Chuen Lung Estate, Route Twisk, Tsuen Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Self-service village tea house in Chuen Lung on the slopes of Tai Mo Shan: you collect your own dim sum and tea and eat on the roof or patio. Har gao, sesame rolls, quail egg siu mai, fried dace balls, stir-fried local watercress and sweet tofu pudding. Why: A hiker's breakfast spot in a Hakka mountain village; rustic plastic-stool dining with countryside views, far from the usual dim sum halls.

Name: One Dim Sum
Location: Shop 1 & 2, G/F, Kenwood Mansion, 15 Playing Field Road, Prince Edward, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: No-reservation dim sum canteen near Prince Edward MTR open until midnight. Known for Chiu Chow-style dumplings, steamed buns with Malaysian sponge cake, and fried shrimp wontons, with items from about HK$20. Why: Cheap, late-hours dim sum that locals queue for; the old Michelin one-star talk is dated, so treat it as a casual neighbourhood favourite.

Name: Maxim's Palace (City Hall)
Location: 2/F, Low Block, City Hall, 5 Edinburgh Place, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cavernous 1960s banquet hall in City Hall serving dim sum from trolleys at lunch, with Sundays and public holidays starting earlier. Classic har gao, siu mai and baked char siu buns in a big, noisy room. Why: Hong Kong's best-known trolley dim sum hall, a living piece of 1960s civic dining; a favourite for family holiday yum cha.

Name: Joy Hing Roasted Meat
Location: 265-267 Hennessy Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Counter-service roast meat shop on the corner of Hennessy and Stewart Roads, known for char siu and roast pork over rice, with roast goose and soy chicken too. Why: A Wan Chai institution for classic char siu rice at street-corner prices; a quick lunch rather than a sit-down meal.

Name: Po Kee
Location: 425P Queen's Road West, Sai Ying Pun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Neighbourhood roast meat shop of 40-plus years that roasts in the factory behind the counter. Lai fan noodles with roast duck leg, roast pork and roast goose; cash only, with goose often gone by mid-afternoon. Why: A Bib Gourmand roast shop favoured by locals over tourist-facing goose restaurants; pre-ordering is possible.

Name: Sang Kee Foods
Location: 263 Queen's Road West, Sai Ying Pun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Chiu Chow marinated-goose shop opened in 1998, braising grain-fed goose in a herb master stock. Order goose slices, blood curd, web, wing, liver and gizzard over rice or noodles. Why: Family-run Chiu Chow braised goose, an everyday Western District favourite that makes use of nearly the whole bird; a counterpoint to Cantonese roast goose.

Name: Yung Kee
Location: 32-40 Wellington Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Multi-floor Cantonese restaurant on Wellington Street, famed for its roast goose. Order the roast goose by half or quarter, with preserved egg and pickled ginger on the side. Why: Hong Kong's most famous roast goose address, a banquet-style institution with prices well above a siu mei counter; fine for a holiday group meal.

Name: Mak's Noodle (Wellington Street)
Location: G/F, 77 Wellington Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Tiny shrimp-wonton noodle shop with the signature small bowl of wontons in a clear, prawn-shell and dried-flounder broth over thin egg noodles. Brisket and noodles with ginger also on the menu. Why: The textbook Cantonese wonton noodle shop, in business since the 1960s and a standard stop for first-time visitors; dainty portions, so pair it with a second bowl.

Name: Ho Hung Kee (Hysan Place)
Location: Shop 1204-1205, 12/F, Hysan Place, 500 Hennessy Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Michelin-starred wonton noodle and congee house that began as a Wan Chai street stall in the 1940s. Springy shrimp-and-pork wontons in sweet broth; the menu also covers congee, dim sum and some Cantonese dishes. Why: A starred noodle shop in a mall, a polished way to try the classic bowl; pricier than a street counter but reliable.

Name: Sister Wah
Location: Shop A1, 13 Electric Road, Tin Hau, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Six-table beef brisket noodle shop now run by the founder's sons. Clear-broth beef trio (brisket, tendon, tripe) noodle soup, plus house-made dumplings, drunken chicken, dan dan noodles and braised radish. Cash only. Why: A micro-sized Bib Gourmand noodle shop that fills when it opens; a local brisket specialist, not a tourist trap.

Name: Kwan Kee Bamboo Noodles
Location: Shop E, 1 Wing Lung Street, Cheung Sha Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Bib Gourmand noodle shop inside a local market that still makes bamboo-pole (zhu sing) noodles by hand. Signature noodles tossed with shrimp roe and oyster sauce; also wonton and soup noodles. Why: One of the few shops left making egg noodles the old bamboo-pole way, in a residential market far from tourist routes. Don't confuse with Kwan Kee Claypot Rice (Sai Ying Pun).

Name: Ho To Tai
Location: 67 Fau Tsoi Street, Yuen Long, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Founded in 1946, one of the few remaining shops that makes its own noodles, in Yuen Long's old town. Wonton soup is the signature; zha jiang noodles, beef brisket noodles and braised radish with shrimp roe also recommended. Why: A traditional New Territories noodle maker with a Bib Gourmand and wonton soup worth the MTR-and-walk trip out to Yuen Long.

Name: Wai Kee Noodle Cafe
Location: 62 Fuk Wing Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Early-opening Sham Shui Po noodle cafe with a loyal line for its pig liver and beef noodle soup, with choice of macaroni, vermicelli or instant noodles plus add-ons of ham, egg or sausage. Kaya French toast on the sweet side. Why: A beloved Sham Shui Po breakfast counter and a cheap local snapshot among the toy and fabric streets; cash only.

Name: Sang Kee Congee Shop
Location: 7 Burd Street, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Old-school congee shop in the Sheung Wan Western Market area. Order the dace fish ball congee (HK$47 in Time Out's 2019 listing), or other fish or century-egg congees with fried dough sticks. Why: A neighbourhood congee house on Burd Street near Sheung Wan's old markets; a simple, cheap breakfast and a lighter alternative to Trusty Congee King.

Name: Cheung Hing Coffee Shop
Location: G/F, 9-11 Yik Yam Street, Happy Valley, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Long-running Happy Valley cha chaan teng with booths and mosaic floor tiles, known for pineapple buns, egg tarts and milk tea. Opens early for breakfast sets. Why: A classic bing sutt-style neighbourhood canteen in Happy Valley, near the racecourse, and a calmer breakfast than Central's chains.

Name: For Kee Restaurant
Location: Shop J-K, 200 Hollywood Road, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Tiny Sheung Wan cha chaan teng known for its 'gold medal' pork chop rice (sweet soy-marinated chop, often with a fried egg), plus tea-restaurant breakfasts and sandwiches. Why: A very local lunch counter on Hollywood Road that hasn't been gentrified; queues of office workers on weekdays.

Name: Sun Heung Yuen
Location: 38A Kweilin Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Sham Shui Po dai pai dong-turned-ice-room on Kweilin Street (the Kin Kee shop). Its egg-and-beef sandwich, milk tea and red bean ice are the classic orders. Distinct from Central's Sing Heung Yuen. Why: One of Sham Shui Po's retro street eateries on the Kweilin Street dai pai dong strip; a cheap breakfast stop between market and fabric streets.

Name: Jin Jin
Location: G/F, Model Housing Estate, 774 King's Road, North Point, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: About 30-year-old Hakka-leaning cha chaan teng in North Point's Model Housing Estate, known for salt-baked chicken (drumstick with noodles or rice), gizzard and liver, and a daily soup. Why: Hakka salt-baked chicken served in a lime-green booth cha chaan teng; a lesser-visited North Point spot in a 1950s model housing estate.

Name: Capital Cafe (Wan Chai)
Location: Shop B1, G/F, Kwong Sang Hong Building, 6 Heard Street, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Retro-styled bing sutt that opened in Wan Chai in 2010. Famous for black truffle scrambled egg toast, butter buns and 'principal's' toast, in a nostalgic room with old-time decor. Why: A revival-style bing sutt that popularised the retro look; more polished than classic street joints and popular with visitors.

Name: Shui Kee Coffee
Location: Shop 17, Cooked Food Centre, 2/F, Sheung Wan Municipal Services Building, 345 Queen's Road Central, Sheung Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Tiny dai pai dong stall in a government cooked-food centre, famous for scrambled-egg sandwiches in hotdog buns or white bread (add ham, corned beef or spam), buttery French toast and cold milk tea in glass bottles. Why: A surviving dai pai dong licence, now indoors on the second floor of a municipal building; cheap, locally loved breakfast and a retro tick for food lovers.

Name: Sing Kee
Location: 82 Stanley Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: One of the few street-side dai pai dong left on Stanley Street, serving big-flame stir-fries. Time Out suggests chilli pepper squid, spare ribs and stir-fried crab. Why: A Bib Gourmand dai pai dong on a lane that survived the 1970s licensing clearances; wok hei outdoors, in the heart of Central.

Name: Oi Man Sang
Location: Shop C, 1 Shek Kip Mei Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Evening dai pai dong-style restaurant next to the Shek Kip Mei estates, open late. Time Out's favourites are salt-and-pepper squid, garlic steamed razor clams, potato and beef stir-fry and salted-egg-yolk prawns. Why: A late-night Sham Shui Po dai pai dong that locals use for big stir-fry dinners; one of the few retro options still going after 23:00.

Name: Keung Kee
Location: 406 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Street-food specialist founded as a stall in 1951 and moved to its Lockhart Road shop in 2021. Order glutinous rice with preserved meat (lo mai fan), wok-fried rice rolls or pork bone congee; add cured Cantonese sausage or duck liver sausage. Why: A 1950s street-stall brand that stayed as a Bib Gourmand cheap eat; a fixture for Wan Chai workers.

Name: Shun Hing (Tai Hang)
Location: G/F, 5 Ormsby Street, Tai Hang, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Tai Hang cha chaan teng-style dai pai dong (cha dong) known for scrambled eggs and char siu rice. Opens early for breakfast and closes mid-afternoon. Why: A small old-school Tai Hang eatery on a residential street near the Fire Dragon area; cheap and local.

Name: Bakehouse (Wan Chai)
Location: 14 Tai Wong Street East, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Artisan bakery started by former Four Seasons pastry chef Gregoire Michaud, famous for its sourdough egg tart with a flaky tangy crust. Also croissants, cookies, doughnuts and pies. The Wan Chai shop is the flagship (2018). Why: A modern, queue-making take on the Hong Kong egg tart, popular with visitors and locals; not retro, but a defining contemporary bakery.

Name: Kadorar Bakery
Location: 1-23 Man Yuen Street, Jordan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Traditional Hong Kong bakery near Temple Street, known for French pudding buns made fresh in the afternoon, alongside classic breads and cakes. Listed 06:30-18:00 or 20:30 by different sources. Why: A neighbourhood old-style bakery between Temple Street and the Jade Market; cheap snack stop in Jordan.

Name: Sang Lung Bakery (San Lung Cake Shop)
Location: 66 Pei Ho Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Old-style Chinese cake shop in Sham Shui Po that bakes traditional items and still hand-bakes mooncakes to order, along with cakes and festive pastries. Why: One of the last handmade Chinese cake shops in Sham Shui Po; picked for traditional pastries rather than a sit-down meal.

Name: Yuk Yip Dessert
Location: 2 Elgin Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Small sweet-soup shop in SoHo selling classic Cantonese desserts such as glutinous rice balls in syrup with peanut and coconut, plus seaweed and mung bean soup, sago and black sesame soup. Priced around HK$20. Why: A very old-school sweet soup stall run by an elderly couple, an inexpensive local alternative in the heart of SoHo.

Name: Yuen Kee Dessert (Tin Hau)
Location: Shop B, Mayson Garden Building, 2A-2E Wing Hing Street, Tin Hau, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Reopened Tin Hau branch of a long-running sweet soup shop that closed its earlier premises in 2023. Sesame soup, sweet almond tea and other hot soups, said to be stone-ground. Why: A winter-friendly sweet soup shop, hot black sesame being the order for December; one of the more traditional dessert rooms on the east side.

Name: Honeymoon Dessert (Sai Kung original)
Location: Po Tung Road, Sai Kung, Hong Kong (G/F, 10A-10C in older listings; moved a few shops along in 2025), Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: First shop of the Hong Kong dessert chain, opened in Sai Kung in 1995. Mango desserts, mango sago pomelo, sweet soups and glutinous rice balls; popular after a seafood meal. Why: The chain's birthplace, still its busiest branch according to Time Out; a mango dessert after a Sai Kung seafood lunch.

Name: Lucky Dessert (Prat Avenue)
Location: 22-24 Prat Avenue, G/F, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong (per a Burpple listing; Wanderlog gives 2 Prat Street), Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Dessert shop on Prat Avenue near Chungking Mansions, known for mango sago and mango waffle with vanilla ice cream. Older reviews praise it as one of the best Hong Kong dessert stalls. Why: A late-opening dessert stop in Tsim Sha Tsui, but the evidence is old; a lesser-known option rather than a priority.

Name: Kung Wo Beancurd Factory
Location: 118 Pei Ho Street, Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Beancurd maker that has made its own tofu since 1893. Michelin calls the silky tofu pudding (dau fu fa) a must-try; also fresh soy milk and fried tofu. Why: A 130-year-old tofu factory and one of Hong Kong's oldest family businesses, with a cheap warm tofu pudding that suits cool December weather.

Name: Cheung Hing Kee Shanghai Pan-fried Buns
Location: G/F, 48 Lock Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Bib Gourmand shop making Shanghai-style pan-fried pork buns (sheng jian bao) with a crisp base and a burst of soup. Flagship on Lock Road in TST; menu extends to shrimp, mala pork, truffle and crab roe buns. Why: A Shanghai-style street snack that has become a Hong Kong favourite; the Lock Road shop is the flagship after beginning in Tsuen Wan.

Name: Fishball Man (To Kwa Wan)
Location: Shop B, G/F, 183 Ma Tau Wai Road, To Kwa Wan, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Fish ball shop in To Kwa Wan serving house-made fish balls with a choice of chilli oil or curry sauce, plus shaomai and cheong fun. Cash only; open from afternoon to the small hours. Why: A Michelin-listed fish ball stall in the 13 Streets area, one of the few places for a real late-night fish ball bowl.

Name: Mammy Pancake (Carnarvon Road)
Location: G/F, Carnarvon Mansion, 8-12 Carnarvon Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Egg waffle (gai daan jai) stall at 8-12 Carnarvon Road near Tsim Sha Tsui MTR. Classic plain egg waffles, plus chocolate and green tea flavours (about HK$20 per Burpple reviews). Why: A well-known egg waffle stall whose Michelin-recommended status made it a TST staple; classic street snack.

Name: Four Seasons Pot Rice
Location: Arthur Street (numbers listed variously as 46-58, 50-52 and 46), Yau Ma Tei, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Evening claypot rice stall-restaurant in Yau Ma Tei, open daily from 18:00 to 01:00. Charcoal-cooked clay pots with Chinese sausage, preserved meats and eel; queues of 45 minutes or more on busy nights. Why: Winter claypot rice cooked to order near Temple Street, one of the late-night places local diners queue for.

Name: Hing Kee Claypot Rice
Location: 15 Temple Street, Yau Ma Tei, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Temple Street claypot rice restaurant with 60-plus varieties cooked on charcoal stoves. Traditional chicken with Chinese sausage is the Michelin pick. Cash only. Why: Classic Temple Street winter food, a decades-old claypot room tied to the night market.

Name: She Wong Leung
Location: Shop A, G/F, 298 Electric Road, North Point, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Snake soup specialist with seasonally adjusted herbal base; set menus pair snake soup with home-style dishes, and double-boiled soups need pre-ordering. Why: A Bib Gourmand snake soup shop, a winter dish at its peak in December (compare Ser Wong Fun in Central).

Name: Megan's Kitchen
Location: 5/F, Lucky Centre, 165-171 Wan Chai Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cantonese home-style restaurant known for hot pots; also steamed minced beef patty with dried mandarin peel and Yu Xiang eggplant in claypot. Why: A 2026 Michelin-listed hot pot room in a Wan Chai commercial block; good for a winter hot pot night.

Name: Under Bridge Spicy Crab
Location: G/F-3/F, Ascot Mansion, 421-425 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Typhoon-shelter style spicy crab restaurant, descended from the tradition of cooking under Causeway Bay's flyovers. Garlic-and-chilli fried crab is the dish; priced high with mixed service reviews. Why: The Causeway Bay flyover spicy crab ritual, now a restaurant; very tourist-oriented and pricey but a recognisable local-style dish.

Name: Hing Kee Restaurant (Typhoon Shelter)
Location: 1/F, Po Wah Commercial Building, 180 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Typhoon-shelter cooking from 16:00 to 02:00: crab stir-fried with garlic and chilli, roast duck soup with flat rice noodles, and boat congee. Seafood comes in limited fresh daily deliveries. Why: A late-night Cantonese seafood restaurant on Nathan Road for after-hours dining; started in Causeway Bay.

Name: Loaf On
Location: 49 See Cheung Street, Sai Kung, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Michelin-starred Sai Kung seafood restaurant. Steamed zebra mantis shrimp on egg-white custard, mantis shrimp with chilli and garlic, and steamed fish with sea salt; some seafood needs pre-ordering. Why: A starred village-style seafood restaurant in Sai Kung, with live market seafood a short walk from the waterfront; a day-trip lunch rather than a Central meal.

Name: Rainbow Seafood Restaurant
Location: G/F, 23-27 First Street, Sok Kwu Wan, Lamma Island, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Waterfront seafood restaurant in Sok Kwu Wan on Lamma. Choose live seafood by weight, cooked Cantonese style; a listing says it offers free ferry shuttles from Central and TST for diners. Why: The classic Lamma seafood day out, with a complimentary ferry from Central or Tsim Sha Tsui for diners (check the current schedule).

Name: Dragon Inn
Location: 12 Tsing Ha Lane, Castle Peak Road, Tuen Mun, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Villa-style Cantonese restaurant in Tuen Mun. Baked baby lobster with cheese is the must-order; also Cantonese barbecue and steamed egg white custard in roasted coconut. Why: A hidden Bib Gourmand house, popular for family banquets, in the western New Territories; far from tourist trails.

Name: Chiuchow Delicacies
Location: Shop 4, G/F, Gain Yu Building, 96 Wharf Road, North Point, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Small Chiu Chow restaurant serving marinated goose and a chilled steamed fish selection, with some dishes needing pre-order and shared tables when busy. Why: A Bib Gourmand Chiu Chow room in North Point; authentic dishes at modest prices.

Name: Hung's Delicacies
Location: Shop B01, Lower Level, Tower 535, 535 Jaffe Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Chiu Chow restaurant that moved from Kwun Tong to Causeway Bay in 2024, centred on marinated goose, offal and a signature fried rice with goose, XO sauce and sakura shrimp. Earned a Bib Gourmand in 2025. Why: Reviving Chiu Chow classics with a Bib Gourmand shortly after opening in Causeway Bay; a modern take on a regional cuisine.

Name: Pang's Kitchen
Location: 25 Yik Yam Street, Happy Valley, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Long-running Happy Valley Cantonese kitchen with a Michelin star. Baked fish tripe omelette in an earthenware pot with Cantonese sausage, snake soup and stir-fried sticky rice. Why: A star on a street of neighbourhood cha chaan tengs; snake soup and home-style Cantonese rather than hushed fine dining.

Name: Sang Kee
Location: 3-4/F, Sunshine Plaza, 353 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cantonese restaurant since 1976 that moved to a brighter, larger room in Sunshine Plaza. Signature salt-baked chicken and baked fish intestine with egg. Why: A Wan Chai landmark since 1976 that kept its menu after moving; Bib Gourmand since 2024.

Name: Wing Lai Yuen
Location: Shop 102-105, 1/F, Gourmet Place, Whampoa Plaza, Site 8, Whampoa Garden, 7 Tak On Street, Hung Hom, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Shanghainese and Sichuan restaurant in Whampoa Garden. Dan dan noodles (spicy or mild, with or without pork) and whole mandarin fish, either Sichuan shuizhu style or sweet and sour. Why: A residential-mall Bib Gourmand, hairy-crab season Shanghainese cooking without the Central price tag.

Name: Yè Shanghai (Tsim Sha Tsui)
Location: Marco Polo Hongkong Hotel, Harbour City, 3 Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Shanghainese fine dining in the Marco Polo Hongkong hotel and a one-star listing in the 2026 Michelin list. Menu details were not retrieved for this branch. Why: A starred Shanghainese room on the Kowloon side near Harbour City, useful if you want a non-Cantonese splurge.

Name: Liu Yuan Pavilion
Location: 3/F, The Broadway, 54-62 Lockhart Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: One-star Shanghainese restaurant with private booths. Sauteed river shrimps, eight treasures in chilli sauce, shredded mandarin fish, drunken squab, xiao long bao and pan-fried pork buns; hairy crab dishes in season. Why: A Michelin-starred Shanghainese room at a mid-high price for Wan Chai; booth seating is prized.

Name: Forum Restaurant
Location: 1/F, Sino Plaza, 255-257 Gloucester Road, Causeway Bay, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Three-star Cantonese restaurant founded in 1977, home of the late Yeung Koon-yat's Ah Yat braised abalone. Also pan-seared leopard coral grouper and baked stuffed crab shell. Why: The abalone king's flagship, three Michelin stars and still a Cantonese institution.

Name: T'ang Court
Location: 1-2/F, The Langham Hong Kong, 8 Peking Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Three-star Cantonese dining at The Langham. Double-boiled Silkie chicken soup with dried scallop and abalone, Peking duck and baked stuffed crab shell. Why: A three-star Cantonese room in a hotel, very difficult to book at short notice around holidays.

Name: The Chairman
Location: 3/F, The Wellington, 198 Wellington Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Michelin-starred Cantonese restaurant focused on local ingredients. Signature steamed crab with Huadiao wine and chicken fat over Chen Cun rice noodles. Bookings open online on certain days; set menus emailed in advance. Why: One of Asia's most celebrated Cantonese restaurants; an expensive splurge with a hard-to-win booking.

Name: Fook Lam Moon (Wan Chai)
Location: 35-45 Johnston Road, Wan Chai, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Veteran Cantonese banquet restaurant with live seafood cooked several ways, deep-fried crispy chicken, baked stuffed crab shell and soup served in a whole winter melon; some dishes need pre-ordering. Why: A decades-old Cantonese luxury institution and one-star holder in Wan Chai.

Name: Duddell's
Location: 3/F, 1 Duddell Street, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Art-filled Cantonese restaurant with a Michelin star. Crispy skin chicken (pre-order) and fried shrimp shreds with conpoy, egg and bean sprouts are the highlights. Why: Cantonese fine dining that doubles as a gallery, a stylish splurge in Central; also has a bar and terrace.

Name: Man Wah
Location: 25/F, Mandarin Oriental Hong Kong, 5 Connaught Road Central, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Cantonese restaurant on the 25th floor of Mandarin Oriental with harbour views and a Michelin star. Duck feet bundled with duck liver, duck meat and char siu (pre-order a day ahead). Why: A hotel Cantonese room with views over Victoria Harbour, held its star for many years.

Name: Mott 32
Location: Basement, Standard Chartered Bank Building, 4-4A Des Voeux Road Central, Central, Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China
Description: Modern Cantonese restaurant in the basement of the Standard Chartered Bank Building. Time Out recommends the Iberico char siu and the roast duck; priced 3 of 4. Why: A sleek Cantonese splurge in Central; not Michelin-starred in the 2026 list I checked.
